translations.title: Complex Computations
translations.explanation: A complex number z=a+bi has real part a and imaginary part b, with i²=−1. Plot z at (a,b) on the complex plane. Its conjugate a−bi is the reflection across the real axis, and its modulus |z|=√(a²+b²) is its distance from the origin. Rectangular and polar forms describe the same point: z=r(cos θ+i sin θ), where r=|z| and θ is the direction from the positive real axis (when z≠0). Geometrically, addition translates vectors; multiplication multiplies moduli and adds arguments. Dividing by a nonzero complex number uses its conjugate to make the denominator real. The distance between z and w is |z−w|, and their midpoint is (z+w)/2. These ideas connect conjugates, polar coordinates, operations and geometry rather than treating complex numbers as symbol manipulation alone.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Conjugate: overline(a+bi)=a−bi. z·overline(z)=a²+b²=|z|²; for z≠0, 1/z=overline(z)/|z|². Rectangular ↔ polar: a=r cos θ, b=r sin θ, r=√(a²+b²); θ must be selected in the correct quadrant. For nonzero z₁ and z₂, |z₁z₂|=|z₁||z₂| and arg(z₁z₂)=arg(z₁)+arg(z₂) modulo 2π. Add/subtract real and imaginary components. Distance d(z,w)=|z−w| and midpoint m=(z+w)/2. The argument of zero is undefined.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1 — conjugate and quotient: z=3+4i. Its conjugate is 3−4i, |z|=5 and 1/z=(3−4i)/25, because (3+4i)(3−4i)=25. Example 2 — plane operations: let w=1+i. Plot z at (3,4) and w at (1,1); their sum 4+5i is the tip of the translated vector, whereas zw=(3+4i)(1+i)=−1+7i. Check |zw|=√50=5√2=|z||w|. Example 3 — coordinate geometry: d(z,w)=|(3+4i)−(1+i)|=|2+3i|=√13. Midpoint (z+w)/2=2+(5/2)i. Example 4 — polar conversion: 3+4i=5(cos θ+i sin θ), where θ=arctan(4/3) lies in quadrant I; multiplying by i rotates this vector 90° counterclockwise to −4+3i.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the real and imaginary parts and draw each number as a point/vector on a labeled complex plane. 2. Use i²=−1 to multiply, or combine components for sums and differences. 3. Conjugate by changing only the imaginary-part sign; multiply conjugate pairs to obtain a²+b². 4. For a quotient, multiply numerator and denominator by the denominator's conjugate, ensuring the denominator is nonzero. 5. To express a complex number in polar form, calculate r, find the quadrant-correct θ and verify r cos θ=a and r sin θ=b. 6. For geometry, subtract complex endpoints and take the modulus for distance; average endpoints for midpoint. 7. Verify a multiplication by checking both algebraic result and modulus/argument.
translations.commonMistakes: Do not treat i² as +1. Conjugation negates b, not the entire complex number. |a+bi| is √(a²+b²), not a+b, a²+b², or |a|+|b|. Never divide by 0+0i. The arctangent of b/a alone may give the wrong quadrant or be undefined when a=0. Addition does not add complex-number arguments. When finding distance subtract endpoints before taking the modulus; the midpoint is the average, not their difference.
translations.quickSummary: Plot a+bi as (a,b). Reflect across the real axis to conjugate; use z·overline(z)=|z|² for reciprocals. Rectangular and polar forms name the same point. Addition uses vector components; multiplication scales/rotates. Distance is |z−w| and midpoint is (z+w)/2.
